name: Marco Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, and nothing goes out with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Jules and I own a 60-hectare farm outside Valden, with a mortgage the size of a small country. We keep 120 outdoor sows, grow potatoes and field vegetables, and sell most of it through our own farm shop and a weekly veg box scheme with about 300 customers. My day starts with the pigs at half six, then it's planting or harvesting depending on the season, and packing boxes on Wednesdays and Thursdays. Jules is a nurse at the district hospital, so the farm is mostly me and two part-time packers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where does technology fit into that day already?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Everywhere I can get it, to be honest. I use an AI assistant every day to plan the box contents from what's ready in the field, answer customer emails, and set the packers' rota. I tried a weeding robot on loan last summer, and it was clumsy but it worked on the carrots. My kids, Luca and Rosa, think it's hilarious that their dad talks to his phone more than to the pigs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, if I'm honest. I'd have liked the weeding robot to get better and cheaper. Online I'd say the hype was overdone but the useful bits are still useful, like the ordering and the emails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't touch me much. The box scheme has a waiting list of forty families, Jules's job is steady, and the farm shop pays the mortgage in a normal year. My worries are the usual ones on a pig farm: a wet autumn, a sick pig, a broken cold store.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the farm as I do now, AI assistant and all. I'd grow the box scheme from 300 to 340 customers by taking families off the waiting list. And I'd still look for a second-hand weeding robot, maybe sharing it with Kemal on the next farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed. A bit flat, maybe, like a promised storm that never came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the farm shop pays the mortgage in a normal year. What happens in a bad one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In a bad year, like the drought two summers ago, we dip into savings and Jules picks up extra shifts. We've about four months put by, and that year we used two of them. It hurts, but it hasn't broken us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you split a weeding robot with, and how?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kemal, who grows onions and leeks next door. We'd go halves, about 9,000 each for a used one, and swap it week by week in spring. He's more careful than me with machines, so I'd make him keep the logbook.

say: The hype was **overdone**, but the useful bits like ordering still help.
I'd have liked **weeding robots** to get better and cheaper.
think: This barely touches me: the **box scheme** has a waiting list of forty.
My worries are the **usual ones**: weather, sick pigs and broken equipment.
do: Grow the box scheme from **300 to 340** customers.
Go halves with Kemal on a **used weeding robot** for about 9,000 each.
Keep using the **AI assistant** for orders, emails and rotas.
feel: **Relaxed** and a bit flat, like a storm that never came.
S0.quote: My worries are the usual ones on a pig farm: a wet autumn, a sick pig, a broken cold store.
fieldNote: Marco sounds **secure**: direct sales, a waiting list and a partner with steady work.
He's **disappointed** that AI stalls, which says a lot about his outlook.
A bad year **dents savings** but he's come through one before.
He plans to **share kit** with a neighbour rather than buy alone.

steps.text: Grow the veg box scheme from 300 to 340 families
Buy a used weeding robot in halves with Kemal next door
Keep planning boxes and rotas with the AI assistant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say great, about time, and I'd say it loudly. Online I'd post about how the AI assistant runs my box scheme, because other small growers should know. But I'd also say the money from all this has to reach farmworkers and small farms, not just the tech firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this is good for me. The thinking side of my farm, the ordering, emails and planning, is maybe a day a week, and AI would cut that to an hour. The hands-on side changes slowly, so I'd have years to bring in robots on my own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand the whole box scheme admin to AI this winter: orders, swaps, delivery routes, the lot. I'd turn the ordering setup into a small paid service for four or five other growers in the co-op, maybe 50 a month each. And I'd book a training day on field robots at the agricultural college in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly. A bit guilty about being excited, because I know people in offices are getting hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you know who'd get hit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Bea does bookings for a holiday company, and that's exactly the job on that card. And Hana, who does our accounts, would probably lose half her small-business clients. I'd keep Hana on even if AI could do our books, because she's been good to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd keep paying Hana when software could do it cheaper. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A farm runs on people who'll come out when it matters, so I'd keep paying our accountant Hana even if software was cheaper. Hana sorted our tax mess in the drought year at no extra charge. I'm all for robots, but I'm not going to be the kind of boss who drops someone the minute a machine is cheaper.

say: This is **about time**, and other growers should hear how it works.
The gains must reach **farmworkers and small farms**, not just tech firms.
think: The **thinking side** of my farm drops from a day a week to an hour.
Hands-on change is slow, so I'd bring in robots **on my terms**.
do: Hand the **box scheme admin** to AI this winter: orders, swaps and routes.
Sell my **ordering setup** to co-op growers for about 50 a month each.
Book a **field robot** training day at the agricultural college in March.
feel: **Excited**, with a bit of guilt about people in offices.
S1.quote: A farm runs on people who'll come out when it matters, so I'd keep paying our accountant Hana even if software was cheaper.
fieldNote: Marco sees Steady Disruption as **good for him** and says so openly.
His progressive side shows in **loyalty to Hana** and worry for office workers.
He spots a **side income** in selling his own ordering setup.
He's calm because his **hands-on core** is safe for years.

steps.text: Hand all box scheme orders, swaps and routes to AI
Sell the ordering setup to co-op growers at 50 a month
Take a field robot training day at the agricultural college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules fast: who owns the robots, who owns the data, and who gets the money. I'd push the growers' co-op to buy robots together so small farms aren't wiped out by the big ones. And I'd tell people to buy from farms they can visit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one scares me a bit, which I didn't expect. By 2031 the big growers have robot farms producing potatoes and veg cheaper than I ever could. My edge is that people know me and trust the box, and I don't know how long trust beats price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before it arrives I'd get the co-op to set up a shared robot fund, and I'd put in 5,000, which is most of our savings. The day AGI lands in 2028 I'd let it run the whole business side, from orders to accounts. Then I'd push the box scheme harder, adding farm visits and a pig-to-plate story that robots can't fake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. I'd sleep badly, but I'd have a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your work is mostly hands-on, and the robots come about three years after AGI. What does that gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those three years are my head start. From 2028 the business side is basically free, so I'd spend all that time getting the co-op's robots and the box scheme ready for 2031. If I waste those three years before the robots come, I'm just a small farm competing with a factory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting most of your savings in is a big risk with a mortgage. How does Jules feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jules would say I'm doing it again, getting excited before the facts are in. We'd agree I put in 3,000 first and the rest after we see the first robot working on a co-op farm. Jules's nursing job is the safe bit of our house, and I wouldn't gamble that.

say: We need **rules now** on who owns the robots, the data and the money.
Small farms should **buy robots together** through the co-op.
think: By 2031 **big robot farms** could grow veg cheaper than I ever could.
My edge is **trust**, and I don't know how long trust beats price.
do: Put **3,000 first**, then more, into a co-op robot fund.
Let AI run **the business side** from the day it arrives in 2028.
Add **farm visits** and a pig-to-plate story to the box scheme.
feel: **Anxious but busy**, sleeping badly but with a list.
S2.quote: If I waste those three years before the robots come, I'm just a small farm competing with a factory.
fieldNote: Marco is **surprised** that the fast picture frightens him.
He reads the gap before robots as a **head start** for the co-op.
His risk-taking is checked by **Jules**, and he accepts a staged plan.
His fear is about **price competition**, not about using the technology.

steps.text: Put 3,000 into a co-op robot fund, more once proven
Let AI run orders and accounts from 2028
Add farm visits to the box scheme to keep customer trust
Push the growers' co-op to buy field robots together

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so no one gets to act surprised. I'd be at the co-op saying this is our window to buy robots together and share the know-how. I'd want the government putting public money into helping small farms through it, the way they once helped with drainage and hedges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd come out of this one all right, maybe better than all right. AGI in 2031 takes my admin, and the robots in 2034 give me years to choose and test the right machines. The worry is still the big robot farms on price, but with eight years I can build the box scheme into something they can't copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend 2027 and 2028 testing every farm robot I can borrow, with Kemal and two other co-op growers. I'd put 2,000 a year into the co-op robot fund instead of one big lump. And I'd start a small farm school day for local families, partly for income and partly so people stay attached to real farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good. A low hum of worry about prices, but I like having a project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep coming back to Kemal and the co-op. Why not just go it alone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a 60-hectare farm can't afford its own fleet of robots, and I'm not proud enough to pretend otherwise. Kemal knows machines, I know software, and Ilse in the co-op knows the buyers. Together we're a decent small company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Luca and Rosa make of the farm in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luca would be 21, and I'd love him to run the robots with me, but I'd never push him. Rosa would be 16 and probably want nothing to do with pigs. My hope is the farm is still ours, still a place they're proud to bring friends.

say: Five years is **fair warning**, so no one can act surprised.
Government should help small farms with **public money**, like drainage grants once did.
think: AGI takes my **admin**, and robots in 2034 give me time to choose well.
The real worry is **big robot farms** competing on price.
do: Test **borrowed farm robots** with Kemal and two co-op growers in 2027 and 2028.
Put **2,000 a year** into the co-op robot fund instead of a lump.
Start a **farm school day** for local families as extra income.
feel: **Mostly good**, with a low hum of worry about prices.
S3.quote: A 60-hectare farm can't afford its own fleet of robots, and I'm not proud enough to pretend otherwise.
fieldNote: With five years' warning Marco becomes **upbeat** and project-minded.
He sees strength in a **co-op team**: machines, software and buyers.
Price pressure from **robot farms** stays on his mind, so he isn't fully calm.
He hopes his children feel **proud** of the farm, without pushing them.

steps.text: Test borrowed farm robots with Kemal and two co-op growers
Put 2,000 a year into the co-op robot fund
Start a farm school day for local families

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best of the AGI pictures, and we should use every year of it. I'd be telling the growers' co-op and anyone who'd listen that ten years is long enough to make robots work for small farms. And I'd push for rules so the big firms can't buy up all the land before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be calm about my own farm here. By 2039 the mortgage is mostly paid, Jules is senior on the wards, and I'd have had a decade to get the robots right. The bit I'd worry about is people who don't have that time, like Bea in her bookings job, who loses out in 2036 no matter what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as now in the first year, using AI every day like I already do. I'd spend a bit on trying new kit each season, maybe a used weeding robot and a feeding system for the sows. And I'd overpay the mortgage by 200 a month so we're nearly clear before robots compete on price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, honestly. It feels like a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture you'd still be cautious about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The land prices. If big firms with robots start buying farms in the 2030s, Kemal or I could get an offer we can't refuse, and then there's no co-op left. I'd want the co-op to agree first refusal on each other's land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your cousin Bea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Bea to come and learn the box scheme with me, half joking and half not. People will still want someone who knows their name and remembers their kid hates beetroot. That's thinking work AI can do, sure, but I think people will pay for it from a person.

say: This is the **best AGI picture**, and every year of it should count.
We need rules so **big firms** can't buy up all the land first.
think: I'd be **calm** about the farm, with the mortgage nearly paid by 2039.
I worry for people with **less time**, like my cousin Bea in bookings.
do: Try **one new machine** each season, starting with a sow feeding system.
Overpay the **mortgage by 200** a month to be nearly clear by 2039.
Get the co-op to agree **first refusal** on members' land.
S4.quote: People will still want someone who knows their name and remembers their kid hates beetroot.
fieldNote: Marco is **calm** here because time, a paid-down mortgage and Jules's job protect him.
His concern turns to **land prices** and big firms buying out the co-op.
He shows care for **his cousin Bea**, whose desk job is far more exposed.
He believes people will still pay for a **human touch** in selling food.

steps.text: Try one new machine each season, starting with sow feeding
Overpay the mortgage by 200 a month until 2039

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because three years isn't long enough for a co-op to buy and learn robots before the big farms have them. What would help is public money for small farms to buy robots together, and rules that stop big firms buying up land while everyone's distracted.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who owns the data. My AI assistant knows every customer, every field and every pig on my farm. If the company behind the assistant owns that, they own more of my farm than the bank does.

headlineQuote: My AI assistant knows every customer, every field and every pig on my farm.
portrait: Marco Costa is a 43-year-old **pig and veg farmer** who sells through his own box scheme.
He uses **AI every day** and wants robots to arrive sooner, not later.
He's calm in the mild pictures and only gets anxious when **AGI comes fast**.
His answer to every threat is **co-op buying** and staying close to customers.
His partner Jules's **nursing job** keeps his risk-taking in check.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because three years is too short for a co-op to get robots before big farms.
whatWouldHelp: **Public money** for small farms to buy robots together.
Rules that stop **big firms** buying up land.
